buildLog.title: Milestone 1: App Shell and Navigation
buildLog.notes:
- Set up the robust navigation skeleton with React Navigation (Native Stack + Bottom Tabs) inside a single Expo Snack compatible app.
- Created central design tokens in `src/theme.js` to enforce consistent 8px grid spacing, high-contrast dark/light accents, and typography.
- Seeded realistic roommate and expense data in `src/data/seedData.js` so placeholder screens immediately show life on first launch.
**Try it:** Launch the app and tap through the bottom tabs (Home, Expenses, Balances, Household) to inspect the shell navigation.

buildLog.title: Milestone 2: Expense Logging & AsyncStorage
buildLog.notes:
- Created `ExpenseContext.js` to manage AsyncStorage persistence for roommates, expenses, and manual settlements.
- Built `ExpenseItem.js` as a reusable component for clean list rendering across screens.
- Updated `AddExpenseScreen.js` with functional form inputs, payer selection, split toggles, and photo URL attachments.
- Upgraded `ExpensesScreen.js` and `ReceiptDetailScreen.js` to consume context and display dynamic expenses and receipts.
**Try it:** Tap "Add Expense" on the overview tab, log a new shared item, and watch it save locally and update balances instantly!

buildLog.title: Milestone 3: Balance Calculation, Settlements & Invite Link
buildLog.notes:
- **Offline Debt Simplification**: Built a robust, local-first debt simplification algorithm that matches debtors and creditors to minimize the total number of transactions.
- **Manual Settlements**: Enabled marking active debts as settled, which appends a settlement record to the local state and recalculates balances instantly.
- **Household Invite Payload**: Created a Base64-encoded state sharing system. Roommates can export their entire household state (roommates, expenses, settlements) into a text payload, share it via any chat app, and import it on another device to sync offline.
- **Polished Empty States & Inline Confirmations**: Added a reusable `EmptyState` component and built inline confirmation flows for settlements to avoid using native-only alert dialogs.

**Try it:** Go to the **Balances** tab to view calculated debts and tap **Settle Up** to record a payment. Then go to the **Household** tab to add a roommate or copy the Base64 invite payload!

data.summary: This file implements the primary dashboard screen where users can view their household financial totals, personal debt balances, and a preview of recent expenses.
data.role: It serves as the main landing screen of the app, connecting global data stores to navigation routes and user interface components.

sections.title: Imports and Data Hookup
sections.explanation: We pull in core React Native UI components, icons, theme configurations, and our central data store. Think of useContext like grabbing the master household key ring so we can access shared expenses and roommate records from anywhere in the house.

sections.title: Computing Dashboard Metrics
sections.explanation: This block calculates live totals, maps out the current user's personal financial balance, and slices the expense list down to the three most recent items. It transforms raw data into bite-sized stats ready for display.

sections.title: Household Summary and Action Buttons
sections.explanation: We render a primary card showing total household spending and your individual balance status, complete with action buttons. Pressing these buttons tells the navigation prop to push a new screen onto your phone's display stack.

sections.title: Recent Expenses List Preview
sections.explanation: This section checks if any expenses exist, displaying a friendly empty state if the list is blank. Otherwise, it loops through the recent items to build clickable rows that lead straight to receipt details.

sections.title: Styles and Layout Rules
sections.explanation: We define visual styling using StyleSheet, managing layout properties like flexbox alignment, card borders, and spacing. This acts as the interior designer blueprint, making sure padding and colors look clean across different phone sizes.

gotchas: Forgetting that JavaScript array slice does not mutate the original array, which is actually helpful here but trips up beginners trying to sort or filter.
Attempting to read properties from roommates or expenses before the context has loaded its initial data, causing undefined errors.
Not providing a unique key prop when mapping over the recent expenses array, which confuses React's virtual DOM reconciliation.

data.summary: This file renders the main expenses screen where users can search through a list of household expenses and tap them for details.
data.role: It sits in the screens directory and serves as a primary view for users interacting with expense data.

sections.title: Imports and Component Setup
sections.explanation: We pull in core React tools, UI components, icons, and our shared data context. Think of Context like a shared bulletin board in the kitchen where everyone can read household notes without asking directly. We also initialize local state to track what the user is typing into the search bar.

sections.title: Filtering Expenses
sections.explanation: This logic takes our full list of expenses and narrows it down based on the search text. By converting both strings to lowercase, we make sure the search is not case-sensitive. It runs on every keystroke to instantly update what the user sees.

sections.title: Search Bar and List Rendering
sections.explanation: Here we return the visual layout, combining a text input for searching and a performance-optimized list component. Think of FlatList as a smart filing cabinet that only draws the folders currently visible on your desk, rather than printing every single folder at once. Each item in the list can also be tapped to navigate to a detailed view.

sections.title: Style Definitions
sections.explanation: We use React Native's StyleSheet to keep our layout rules organized and separate from the markup. Reusing values from our theme file helps maintain a consistent look and feel across the entire app.

gotchas: Forgetting to supply a keyExtractor to a FlatList, which forces React to guess item identities and can cause severe rendering bugs.
Performing heavy calculations or network requests directly inside the render loop instead of wrapping them in hooks.

data.summary: This screen provides a form to create a new shared expense, allowing users to enter a description, amount, select who paid, and choose who to split it with.
data.role: It is a form screen navigated to from the main dashboard when a user wants to record a new bill.

sections.title: Imports and State Setup
sections.explanation: We pull in core React hooks and context tools, then set up local variables to hold the form data like title and amount. Think of this like setting up the blank fields on a paper ledger before you start writing.

sections.title: Validation and Submission
sections.explanation: Before saving, we verify that the user typed a description and a valid number for the amount. If everything checks out, we send the data up to our shared app context and pop back to the previous screen.

sections.title: Inputs and Dynamic Roommate Pills
sections.explanation: This block renders scrollable form fields and maps over the roommates list to create interactive selection buttons. It is like generating a custom checklist of people dynamically depending on how many roommates live in the house.

sections.title: Receipt Preview and Styles
sections.explanation: If a receipt image link is provided, an image component renders a preview directly below the input field. The StyleSheet at the bottom organizes colors, padding, and layout rules using our design theme.

gotchas: Forgetting that TextInput values are always strings, meaning you must parse them into numbers before performing math or saving financial records.
Mutating state arrays directly instead of using spread syntax or filter, which breaks React's ability to detect changes and re-render the screen.

data.summary: This file calculates roommate financial balances, simplifies who owes what, and renders the user interface for tracking shared expenses.
data.role: Screen component that acts as the financial dashboard for the app.

sections.title: Debt Calculation Engine
sections.explanation: This pure JavaScript function processes all expenses and manual payouts to figure out who owes money and who should receive it. Think of it like balancing a group ledger at the end of a vacation to find the fewest transactions needed to settle up.

sections.title: Component Setup and State Access
sections.explanation: The screen component grabs global data like roommates and expenses using React context, then runs the calculation function to get active balances. It also provides a handler function to record new settlements when a payment is made.

sections.title: Balances and Debts Rendering
sections.explanation: This block loops through the roommates and active debts to display each person's financial standing on the screen. If no one owes anything, it renders an encouraging empty state component instead.

sections.title: Settlement History and Styling
sections.explanation: It renders a chronological log of past payments made between roommates at the bottom of the screen. The StyleSheet object below defines all visual properties like padding, colors, and layout rules.

gotchas: Modifying global context values directly instead of using the provided handler functions like addSettlement.
Forgetting that JavaScript floating-point math can lead to tiny decimal inaccuracies, which is why the code uses 0.01 tolerance checks.
Not wrapping lists in a ScrollView or FlatList when content exceeds screen height, causing items to clip off-screen.

data.summary: The SettingsScreen manages household roommates and handles offline data synchronization via Base64 encoded state strings.
data.role: It serves as the configuration hub of the app, allowing users to update household members and share state without a backend server.

sections.title: Imports and Context Hook
sections.explanation: This block imports core React Native building blocks and hooks into our global state using useContext. Think of useContext like grabbing the master TV remote from the coffee table instead of walking over to the television for every button press. Local state variables are also set up here for handling text inputs and status feedback banners.

sections.title: Roommate Management Logic
sections.explanation: Here we define the function to add new roommates to our household array. It validates that the input isn't empty, creates a unique ID using a timestamp, and calls our global save function. A temporary banner helper is also provided to flash success or error messages.

sections.title: State Serialization and Sharing
sections.explanation: This section serializes the entire household state into a JSON string and encodes it into Base64 format so it can be safely sent as text. The native Share API then opens your operating system's share sheet. It is like packing an entire room into a cardboard box of text so you can mail it to a friend.

sections.title: State Import and Deserialization
sections.explanation: This code takes a pasted Base64 string from your clipboard, decodes it back into text, and parses it into JavaScript objects. If the format checks out, it overwrites the current household state through the global context. Always validate imported data structures carefully before accepting them to prevent app crashes.

sections.title: Settings UI Layout
sections.explanation: The render method builds a scrollable view containing status alerts, input forms for roommates, and action buttons for syncing. We map over the roommates array to display each user dynamically with custom avatars and tags. This forms the visual interface the user interacts with directly.

gotchas: Forgetting to handle UTF-8 characters properly when using btoa and atob, which can corrupt names containing emojis or special accents.
Not validating the structure of imported JSON data, leading to app crashes if a user pastes malformed text.
Mutating the roommates array directly using push() instead of passing a brand new array reference into saveRoommates.

data.summary: This file displays the detailed view of a selected expense, including who paid, metadata, an attached receipt image, and an option to delete it.
data.role: It sits in the screens layer, acting as a detail view pushed onto the navigation stack when a user taps an expense item.

sections.title: Imports and Component Setup
sections.explanation: We pull in core React Native UI components alongside navigation props and global context data. Think of route.params like opening a specific file handed to you in a folder, containing the details of the exact expense you tapped.

sections.title: Render UI and Conditional Receipt
sections.explanation: This block structures the layout, showing text details at the top and conditionally rendering either the receipt image or a fallback placeholder if none exists. Using logical operators like the question mark prevents crashes if data hasn't loaded yet.

sections.title: Style Sheet Definitions
sections.explanation: We use StyleSheet.create to organize all our visual rules in one place, keeping components clean and optimized. It behaves much like CSS, but tailored specifically for mobile layouts.

gotchas: Forgetting to check if route.params exists can cause the app to crash if the screen is somehow accessed without an expense object.
Not providing width and height dimensions to the Image component will cause remote or local URI images to fail to render.
Typos in style property names like alignItem instead of alignItems fail silently without throwing a standard JS error.

data.summary: App.js is the root entry point of SplitFlat, setting up global navigation, visual styling, and data context for the entire application.
data.role: Application entry point and routing coordinator. Think of this file as the main floor manager of a building, directing users to the right rooms (screens) and supplying everyone with the tools they need (state and theme).

sections.title: Imports and Setup
sections.explanation: We bring in React Native packages, icons, screen components, and navigation tools. We also instantiate our navigator objects which will handle moving between screens.

sections.title: Tab Navigator
sections.explanation: This function defines the bottom navigation bar you see at the bottom of the app. It dynamically assigns icons based on whether a tab is currently focused by the user.

sections.title: Root Component
sections.explanation: This component wraps our entire app in wrappers like SafeAreaProvider to prevent content from hiding under phone notches, and ExpenseProvider so every screen can read and write expense data.

gotchas: Placing hooks or data-fetching logic directly inside App.js instead of delegating them to screens or context providers.
Forgetting to wrap the app in NavigationContainer, which causes React Navigation to throw a runtime error.
Mixing up stack navigation and tab navigation hierarchies.

data.summary: This file creates a global data store for expenses, roommates, and settlements, handling both local React state and permanent offline storage.
data.role: It sits at the core of the data layer, allowing any screen in the app to read or update app data without passing props manually.

sections.title: Context Creation and Storage Keys
sections.explanation: We create a React Context which acts like a magical broadcast channel for our app data. Think of it like a community bulletin board where any component can read or post updates. We also define distinct string keys to keep our local storage organized.

sections.title: Provider State and Initial Load
sections.explanation: The provider component holds our app's core state and loads saved data from the device storage when the app first opens. AsyncStorage acts like a mini hard drive for your phone, storing text data even when the app is closed.

sections.title: Persistence Helper Functions
sections.explanation: These helper functions update the React state and immediately save the new data into device storage. Because storage only accepts text strings, we convert our JavaScript objects into text using JSON.stringify.

sections.title: Data Mutation Actions
sections.explanation: These functions handle adding new expenses, deleting items, and importing household states. They keep our data predictable by ensuring every new entry gets a unique ID and a timestamp before saving.

sections.title: Providing the Context Value
sections.explanation: We wrap our child components in the Context Provider and pass down all our state variables and functions. Any screen nested inside this provider can now access this data instantly.

gotchas: Forgetting that AsyncStorage operations are asynchronous and failing to await them, leading to race conditions where UI updates before the data is saved.
Trying to store raw JavaScript arrays or objects directly into AsyncStorage instead of converting them to strings using JSON.stringify first.

learning.overview: Welcome to your personalized learning path for SplitFlat! Based on the code in your repository, we have curated 4 key concepts spanning from foundational component styling and navigation to global state management and persistent offline storage. Each lesson includes code references from your project, a micro-lesson, interactive quiz questions, and a targeted coding challenge.

lessons.whyInYourApp: SplitFlat relies on StyleSheet for clean, scalable visual styling across all screens and reusable UI components, ensuring consistent spacing, border radii, and color tokens from your theme.
lessons.lesson:
In React Native, layout and styling are handled through JavaScript objects passed to `StyleSheet.create()`. Unlike the web, React Native uses a subset of CSS where properties are camelCased (e.g., `backgroundColor` instead of `background-color`) and flexbox is enabled by default with `flexDirection: 'column'` as the default orientation.

To build maintainable mobile apps, it is a best practice to centralize design tokens—such as color palettes, spacing metrics, and typography sizes—into a dedicated theme file. Components can then reference these tokens dynamically. For example, creating a card container involves combining flexbox properties, border radius tokens, and subtle shadow properties for iOS and Android elevation.

In SplitFlat, you use `src/theme.js` to define global design constants like `theme.colors.primary` and `theme.spacing.md`, which are imported across screens and components like `DebtCard.js` and `HomeScreen.js` to guarantee consistent visual hierarchy and branding.

quiz.question: What is the default flexDirection in React Native flexbox layouts?
quiz.explanation: Unlike standard web CSS where block elements stack vertically by default, React Native's default flex direction is 'column', meaning child elements stack top-to-bottom.

quiz.question: Why is StyleSheet.create preferred over inline style objects in React Native?
options: It is required to render Text components on Android.
It automatically converts CSS to native views without JavaScript bridge overhead.
It enables style optimization and identifier caching by passing numeric references across the bridge.
It allows the use of media queries.
quiz.explanation: StyleSheet.create processes and validates styles on startup, assigning integer references so only IDs are passed across the React Native bridge during renders rather than full style objects.

challenge.task: Add a new color token 'info' to theme.js under colors and use it in a card border.
challenge.hint: Open src/theme.js, add info: '#3B82F6' under the colors object, and reference it in one of your screens.
challenge.successCriteria: The app compiles successfully and the new color token can be imported without errors.

lessons.whyInYourApp: SplitFlat uses bottom tabs to let users instantly toggle between core household views: Overview, Expenses, Balances, and Household Settings.
lessons.lesson:
Mobile applications often use bottom tab navigation for top-level routing, allowing users to switch context between distinct functional areas with a single tap. In React Navigation, this is achieved using `@react-navigation/bottom-tabs`.

Tab navigators maintain the state of each tab screen by default, preserving scroll positions and form inputs when switching back and forth. You can customize tab appearance by configuring `screenOptions`, where callbacks receive route objects to dynamically render icons using vector icon libraries like `@expo/vector-icons`.

In SplitFlat's `App.js`, `MainTabs` sets up four primary tabs (`HomeTab`, `ExpensesTab`, `BalancesTab`, and `SettingsTab`). Each tab features customized active/inactive color tinting and conditional icon rendering based on focus state, providing intuitive visual feedback to roommates navigating household expenses.

quiz.question: What happens to a screen's local state when you switch away from it in a Bottom Tab Navigator by default?
options: The app crashes due to unhandled memory leaks.
The screen component unmounts and all state is destroyed.
The screen reloads its seed data automatically.
The screen remains mounted in the background, preserving its state and scroll position.
quiz.explanation: By default, React Navigation's bottom tabs keep mounted screens alive in the background so their state and scroll offset are preserved when switching tabs.

quiz.question: How do you pass dynamic props like active icon states into tab bar icons?
options: Using the render callback parameters ({ focused, color, size }) provided by screenOptions.
By querying the DOM element tree.
By reading from the screen's route params.
quiz.explanation: The tab bar icon option accepts a function that receives an object with focused, color, and size properties to style icons appropriately.

challenge.task: Change the active tab bar tint color in App.js to use theme.colors.primaryDark.
challenge.hint: In App.js inside MainTabs screenOptions, locate tabBarActiveTintColor and change it.
challenge.successCriteria: The active tab icon and label render with the darker primary color.

lessons.whyInYourApp: SplitFlat uses React Context to share expenses, roommates, and settlement records globally across Home, Expenses, Balances, and Settings screens without prop drilling.
lessons.lesson:
As mobile applications grow beyond simple single-screen prototypes, multiple components often need access to the same core data—such as user profiles, shopping carts, or financial transactions. Passing props down through every intermediate component layer (prop drilling) quickly becomes unmaintainable.

React Context solves this by providing a way to share values globally across the component tree without explicitly passing props at every level. It consists of two primary parts: `createContext` to establish the data channel, and a Provider component that wraps child nodes and supplies state and action handlers via the `value` prop. Consumer components then access this data instantly using the `useContext` hook.

In SplitFlat, `src/context/ExpenseContext.js` acts as the central data store. It holds the `expenses`, `roommates`, and `settlements` arrays, and exposes methods like `addExpense`, `deleteExpense`, and `addSettlement` so any screen can update household records seamlessly.

quiz.question: What is the primary problem solved by React Context?
options: Prop drilling through deeply nested component trees
quiz.explanation: React Context eliminates prop drilling by allowing any component in the provider tree to consume shared state directly.

quiz.question: Which hook is used to consume values from a React Context in a functional component?
quiz.explanation: useContext accepts a context object created by createContext and returns the current context value.

challenge.task: Expose the total expense count from ExpenseContext so it can be consumed in SettingsScreen.
challenge.hint: In ExpenseContext.js, include expenses.length in the context value object.
challenge.successCriteria: Any component consuming ExpenseContext can read the total expense count.

lessons.whyInYourApp: SplitFlat is offline-first, using AsyncStorage to persist household expenses and roommate balances locally on the device so data remains intact across app restarts.
lessons.lesson:
Mobile apps must handle app closures and device reboots gracefully. While web apps rely heavily on cloud databases or localStorage, React Native applications running locally require persistent key-value storage solutions such as `@react-native-async-storage/async-storage`.

AsyncStorage is an asynchronous, unencrypted, persistent storage system. Because all reads and writes are asynchronous operations returning Promises, data persistence logic is typically wrapped inside `useEffect` hooks upon component mount and triggered whenever state mutations occur. Since AsyncStorage only stores string key-value pairs, complex JavaScript objects and arrays must be serialized using `JSON.stringify()` before saving and parsed back with `JSON.parse()` upon retrieval.

In SplitFlat, `ExpenseContext.js` integrates AsyncStorage to save expenses, roommates, and settlements whenever changes happen. This ensures that roommates can track shared household bills offline without fear of data loss when closing the app.

quiz.question: What format must data be converted into before storing it in AsyncStorage?
quiz.explanation: AsyncStorage accepts string keys and string values only, so objects and arrays must be serialized using JSON.stringify().

quiz.question: Why are AsyncStorage methods asynchronous?
options: To synchronize data instantly with cloud servers.
To comply with HTTP REST API standards.
To prevent blocking the React Native JavaScript thread during disk I/O operations.
quiz.explanation: Disk storage operations are asynchronous to prevent blocking the single-threaded JavaScript execution loop, keeping UI animations smooth.

challenge.task: Add a AsyncStorage clear function in ExpenseContext to reset local data back to seed state.
challenge.hint: Use AsyncStorage.multiRemove([STORAGE_KEYS.EXPENSES, STORAGE_KEYS.ROOMMATES]) inside a reset function.
challenge.successCriteria: Calling the reset function clears stored keys and resets state back to initial values.
